note: Addresses when an updated system is still the same system, which decides whether re-assessment is triggered and is rarely documented by clients.
title: High-Risk AI Systems and the Problem of Identity in the European AI Act
explain_beginner: The European Union has rules for high-risk AI systems. These rules assume we can tell when an updated system is still the same system, because that decides whether it must be checked again. The paper says the law does not clearly explain how to make that call. The author proposes a way to judge identity using what a system is meant to do and how trustworthy it is. This matters because without a clear test, companies and regulators may disagree about when new checks are needed.
explain_business: Under the EU AI Act, high-risk systems face checks before launch, monitoring after launch, and fresh assessment when substantially modified. Each step requires deciding whether an updated system is still the same system, yet the law gives no clear internal test. This paper offers a practical lens based on intended function and trustworthiness, plus a simple decision flow for audits and disputes. For executives, it signals that identity decisions should be documented and defensible. It informs investment in precise intended purpose reporting and standardized trustworthiness reporting, which support comparability across time and deployments.
explain_practitioner: The paper examines identity judgments under the EU AI Act, which requires conformity assessment, post-market monitoring, and re-assessment after substantial modification. The author applies the function+ framework, individuating systems by intended function plus context-sensitive trustworthiness criteria. The analysis finds the Act lacks an internal auditable test for synchronic identity, meaning sameness at a single point in time, and defers this to sectoral or harmonization instruments. The contribution maps AIA lifecycle obligations to function+ components and offers a minimal decision flow for audits and disputes, plus recommendations for testable intended purpose and standardized trustworthiness reporting.
